name: Iahub and Xors
description: Iahub does not like background stories, so he'll tell you exactly what this problem asks you for. You are given a matrix a with n rows and n columns. Initially, all values of the matrix are zeros. Both rows and columns are 1-based, that is rows are numbered 1, 2, ..., n and columns are numbered 1, 2, ..., n . Let's denote an element on the i -th row and j -th column as a i , j . We will call a submatrix ( x 0 , y 0 , x 1 , y 1 ) such elements a i , j for which two inequalities hold: x 0 ≤ i ≤ x 1 , y 0 ≤ j ≤ y 1 . Write a program to perform two following operations: Query( x 0 , y 0 , x 1 , y 1 ): print the xor sum of the elements of the submatrix ( x 0 , y 0 , x 1 , y 1 ) . Update( x 0 , y 0 , x 1 , y 1 , v ): each element from submatrix ( x 0 , y 0 , x 1 , y 1 ) gets xor-ed by value v .
input_specification: The first line contains two integers: n ( 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000 ) and m ( 1 ≤ m ≤ 10 5 ). The number m represents the number of operations you need to perform. Each of the next m lines contains five or six integers, depending on operation type. If the i -th operation from the input is a query, the first number from i -th line will be 1. It will be followed by four integers x 0 , y 0 , x 1 , y 1 . If the i -th operation is an update, the first number from the i -th line will be 2. It will be followed by five integers x 0 , y 0 , x 1 , y 1 , v . It is guaranteed that for each update operation, the following inequality holds: 0 ≤ v < 2 62 . It is guaranteed that for each operation, the following inequalities hold: 1 ≤ x 0 ≤ x 1 ≤ n , 1 ≤ y 0 ≤ y 1 ≤ n .
output_specification: For each query operation, output on a new line the result.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 341D — Iahub and Xors [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
